source.title: A concept-aware explainability method for convolutional neural networks
source.authors: M. Gürkan; N. Arıca; F. Yarman-Vural

page_placements.theme: Measured interpretability depends on the labelling tool, metric, threshold, concept vocabulary, probing data and explainer

record.tranche_reason: The study compares concept-to-filter explainability methods on CNNs and reports how many filters each method associates with at least one concept. This is a different measure from the claim’s estimates of interpretable-neuron shares, but bears on its tool-related component in V4.
record.gate_note: The reported number of detecting filters (Table 3) bears on whether tool choice changes the share of filters associated with concepts. The number of unique detected concepts (Table 2) is not a measure of interpretable-filter share and is not included as a row. The explanation examples and concept-recall/F1 results assess other aspects of CAE, not the claim versions. The study does not validate whether a filter’s assigned concept predicts its activations on held-out examples.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a concept-to-filter labelling method (CAE) and benchmarks it against NetDis, Net2Vec and CLIP-Dissect. It uses 'number of detecting filters' and 'number of unique detectors' as performance metrics for the methods. It does not estimate what share of filters have one coherent, validated job. CAE keeps the top Z=30 concepts for every filter (Sect. 2.3, 3.3), so it assigns concepts to all 512 filters by construction. A 512/512 count therefore reflects the method's design, not neuron interpretability. The paper never checks whether assigned concepts are a filter's main job or predict its firing. No architecture, regularization or InceptionV1 comparison is made. This is a method comparison, not a test of V4 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that CAE outperforms NetDis, Net2Vec and CLIP-Dissect on unique detectors and detecting filters, and that it associates nearly all concepts with multiple filters. They report that explanation reports help justify correct and wrong predictions and that the method can compare models. They note limits: a 200-concept dictionary, segmentation and labelling quality, sample imbalance, and a need for more models. The paraphrase should add that the authors present filter coverage as method performance, not as a claim about how interpretable the networks are.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes CAE, a concept-to-filter association method based on masked activations and detection-score means; it compares its filter-coverage counts with existing methods rather than reproducing the neuron-pole audit or testing explanation fidelity on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Filter coverage changes with the explainability method and, for NetDis and Net2Vec, across the four model/training-dataset combinations.

fits_no_version.finding: How many final-layer CNN filters receive any concept label depends strongly on the labelling method. NetDis labels 395–484 of 512 filters and Net2Vec 191–512, while CLIP-Dissect and CAE label all 512 (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The count of 'concept-detecting' units in a CNN layer depends on the dissection method's thresholding and assignment rules. Coverage counts alone are not evidence of how interpretable neurons are.

record.problems: The count of concept-associated filters is only a proxy for interpretability: the study does not test whether the assigned concepts predict activations on held-out examples. The authors report that the dictionary contains only 200 concepts, has sample imbalance and occasional labeling issues, and that further models and more robust data are needed.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's number-of-unique-detectors results were omitted because they count concepts identified, not the share of filters associated with concepts. Explanation-example, report-recall and F1 results were omitted because they do not measure the claim's interpretable-filter share.

untested.parts: All: language models, dense vs mixture-of-experts models, scale.
All: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization.
Share of interpretable neurons, the effect of architecture or regularization, InceptionV1-sized estimates. Coverage counts of concept labels per method do not measure interpretability.
All: attribution graphs from neurons, replacement models.
Whether explanations predict where filters fire. Not tested.
All: simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels should be dropped. Full coverage by CAE and CLIP-Dis follows from their assignment rules: CAE keeps the top-30 concepts per filter regardless of strength. So 512/512 says nothing about whether filters have one main job. Report recall is only 17–26% (Table 10), and the paper flags concept-similarity confusions and faulty explanations. These suggest the per-filter labels are loose, but the paper does not test them against firing behaviour.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level job counts and the shares of single-job, related multi-job, or not-yet-understood poles.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.

The study measures concept-detecting filters for four CNNs, but does not estimate the proportion of human-interpretable neurons, test architecture or regularization as causes, or assess InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs, behavioral explanation, replacement models, and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples predict where a unit fires.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.problem: Value fine; it is the study's own method, so arguably should not be a row (verdict_rules section 2).

relation.reason: CAE builds on filter-concept association and assumes a limited number of concepts activate each filter. It reports only its own method's performance and does not test the claim. The reader's 'tests' is wrong.

tranche.reason: The paper proposes CAE and benchmarks coverage counts (unique detectors, detecting filters) against NetDis, Net2Vec and CLIP-Dissect. It does not estimate the share of clean or interpretable neurons, and it does not validate per-filter labels. T4 fits (T6 is also arguable). The reader's T2 is wrong.

source_check.notes: The Table 3 header text is garbled. The column order (R18-Places, VGG-Places, R18-ImageNet, VGG-ImageNet) matches Table 1 and the text's Dis-CAE vs VGG remark. Counts measure coverage, not interpretability. CAE's 512 is close to automatic, since Y=Z=30 truncation gives every filter concepts. All 10 rows are method-comparison rows (comparator methods or the study's own method).

statements.correction: Table 3 (final conv layer, 512 filters): NetDis 395-484; Net2Vec 191-512; CLIP-Dis (cos and swpmi), Dis-CAE and CAE 512 on all four models. Counts are filters detecting at least one concept, a coverage metric.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CAE and Dis-CAE on the four tested CNNs
reader_labels.reason: All 512 filters are reported as detecting at least one concept with these methods, consistent with higher concept-association coverage using these tools (T3-R17–T3-R24). This supports only the coverage component, not validated interpretability.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: NetDis and Net2Vec across the four tested CNNs
reader_labels.reason: The number of filters associated with concepts varies by method and model, and some counts are below 512, so coverage is not uniformly high across tools and settings (T3-R01–T3-R08).
